meta.blurb: Leila wins every argument and still feels empty. Over one summer at an old harbour boatyard, a retired boat builder teaches her to notice the proud, defensive voice inside her, and to hold it more lightly.
meta.bible: Leila Haddad: a clever, busy team leader of about thirty-four who always needs to be right. Mr Okafor: a retired boat builder with white hair and patient hands, who teaches without preaching. Dan: her colleague and rival. Priya: a young colleague, kind and quick with ideas. Sami: Leila's younger brother. Leila's mother visits once. The story takes place in one seaside town over one summer, from June to September. The old Boatyard on Harbour Lane has a small wooden boat that Mr Okafor repairs. Key terms: Ego means here the picture or image of oneself that feels it must be defended, not Freud's technical term, and the book says so. Lawyer is Leila's name for the defensive inner voice. Labels, Roles, Comparison, Envy, Pride, Humility, Awe, Curiosity, Credit. Many contemplative and philosophical traditions, including Buddhist, Christian, Sufi and Stoic teachers, speak in their own words about loosening self-importance; the book credits them in general terms and never ranks them. The science is hedged: some studies suggest awe and kind attention make people less self-focused, but results vary. Voice and tone: warm, practical, concrete, gently humorous; one clear idea in each beat; no claim that anything cures everything; Mr Okafor never preaches.

B1B2: Leila has just won an argument in a long meeting, and everyone in the room knows it. Yet on the walk home she feels strangely empty, as if she has won something that was never worth having.
In bed that night, Leila goes through the meeting again and again. She changes a word here and adds a clever answer there, although nobody is listening but herself.
The next morning, Dan thanks Priya in front of the whole team for a clever idea. Leila is sure that the idea started with her, and she feels her face grow hot.
On Saturday she walks down to the harbour to clear her head. There she meets Mr Okafor, an old boat builder, who is sanding the side of a small wooden boat.
Leila finds herself telling him the whole story, although she hardly knows him. When she has finished, he says nothing for a while, and then he asks who it was that felt so hurt.
Mr Okafor explains that everyone carries a picture of who they are. People often call it the ego, although psychologists use that word in other ways, and here it simply means the self-image.
A small child learns a name, a place in the family and what earns a smile. Slowly, from praise and from comparison with others, a picture of the self begins to grow.
Mr Okafor asks Leila to write down the words she uses to describe herself. She fills a whole page with labels, and the top three are clever, reliable and right.
Mr Okafor points out that a picture which feels fragile has to be guarded all day long. Every small insult becomes an attack, and every small success becomes a repair.
The self-image always wants to measure itself against other people. It either feels better than them or worse than them, but in both cases the attention stays on the self.
Comparison is like a ladder with no top at all. Whatever rung you reach, somebody is always standing one step above you, and that thought can spoil the whole climb.
Opinions can feel like parts of our own body. When someone disagrees, we feel attacked, so we fight to defend an idea as though it were an arm or a leg.
Mr Okafor gives her a task for the week. She does not have to change anything or fight the voice in her head, but only to notice what it says.
On the bus on Monday, Leila notices something she has never seen before. Without meaning to, she is judging the people around her by their shoes, their phones and their faces.
At her desk, Leila notices the story she tells about Dan: he is selfish, and he is against her. She realises that it is only a story, and a thought is not the same as a fact.
Mr Okafor suggests that she give the voice a name, which makes it easier to see. Leila calls it the Lawyer, because it always defends her and never looks for the truth.
The Lawyer always speaks for Leila and never speaks for anyone else. It collects every piece of evidence in her favour, but it does not ask whether the other person might have a point.
Mr Okafor teaches her a very small trick: take one slow breath before you reply. In that short gap, she can choose what to say instead of letting the Lawyer speak first.
Her younger brother Sami phones to complain about his job. Leila usually gives him a lecture, but this time she takes a breath and simply listens.
Mr Okafor says that many of us listen only while we wait for our turn to speak. Real listening needs open space inside, and that space is hard to find when we are busy being clever.
Leila gets a kind email from a client, and she glows for an hour. Then the feeling fades, and she finds that she wants another one, which shows her how praise works.
At work, a manager criticises Leila's report, and it stings badly. Instead of defending herself, she asks one calm question: is there anything in this that is true?
Mr Okafor tells Leila about his first boatyard, which failed when he was young. He had been too proud to admit that he did not understand the accounts, and so the debts grew in silence.
The next day, Leila swallows her pride and asks Priya to help her with a difficult spreadsheet. It feels like admitting defeat, and her heart beats a little faster.
Priya is delighted to be asked, and the two women end up laughing together. Leila learns that asking for help does not make her smaller, and it gives other people a chance to feel useful.
An old friend is given a big promotion, and Leila feels a sharp pang of envy. She does not pretend that it is not there, but she looks at it as honestly as she can.
When she watches the envy without feeling guilty, it begins to tell her something. It points to what she truly wants, and that is information she can use, not a judgement on her character.

Mr Okafor says that humility is often misunderstood by almost everyone. It does not mean thinking badly of yourself, but thinking about yourself less, so that more of your attention is free for the world.
Leila had always believed that being hard on herself made her stronger. Mr Okafor points out that harsh self-hatred keeps all the attention on me, and so it is the same trap with a gloomier face.
At work, Leila sends an important report to a client and finds, an hour later, that one figure is wrong. Her stomach drops, and the Lawyer immediately begins to look for someone else to blame.

This time Leila takes a slow breath and lets the Lawyer finish its speech without believing it. Then she writes to the client, admits her mistake plainly, and offers the right number with a short apology.
To her surprise, the client is not angry at all. He thanks her for telling him quickly, and he says that he trusts a person who admits mistakes more than one who never makes any.
In the next meeting, Leila gives Priya full credit for a good piece of analysis. She expects to feel smaller, but instead she feels lighter, and the room seems warmer than before.
Mr Okafor says that no boat builder has ever controlled the sea. The old Stoic teachers made the same point long ago, when they said that some things are up to us and many are not.
Leila's mother comes to stay with her for a whole weekend. Within an hour, Leila is behaving like a fifteen-year-old, and she is snapping at the smallest remark about her cooking.
Mr Okafor says that roles are useful, because the world needs managers, daughters and friends. The trouble starts only when we forget that a role is something we do, and not all that we are.
News arrives that her company is planning a reorganisation. Nobody knows who will keep their jobs, and Leila feels her old fears rising, especially the fear of losing her title.
Leila asks herself what would remain if the title and the labels were taken away. After a long walk, she writes three answers: what she values, whom she cares about, and what she pays attention to.

Under the fear of losing her job lies a deeper one, which is the fear of being nobody. Yet Leila notices that she is standing here, breathing, thinking and caring, and that already seems like quite a lot.
At dawn, Mr Okafor asks Leila to row out of the harbour with him. For a long time they say nothing, and there is only the sound of the oars and the water.

Out on the water, the sky is enormous, and Leila feels very small. Strangely, this does not frighten her, and it feels like relief, because some studies suggest that awe turns our attention outward and makes us kinder.

Leila asks Mr Okafor a hard question about the sea, and he simply says that he does not know. She notices that the words make him look more trustworthy, and not less, and she decides to try them herself.
One evening Leila stays late and sands a long plank of the old boat, with nobody watching. She will not tell anyone, and she is surprised how deeply she enjoys the quiet work.

In a tense team meeting, Leila says out loud that she was wrong about a plan. She had feared that people would lose respect for her, but instead the room relaxes and the discussion becomes more honest.
A few days later, Leila is tired and late, and she snaps rudely at a stranger in a long queue. She goes home ashamed, and she wonders whether all her work this summer has been for nothing.
Leila tells Mr Okafor about the queue, and he only laughs kindly. He says that falling back is part of the practice, and that the only thing to do is to forgive yourself and begin again.

Mr Okafor says that nobody can throw the ego away, and the aim is to hold it lightly, like a rope in the hand. Many traditions, from Buddhist to Christian and Sufi, teach the same thing in their own words.
The reorganisation is finally announced, and Leila is offered a new role leading a smaller team. She would once have counted every rung of her title, but now she asks only whether the work is good.
At the end of summer, the little wooden boat is finished and launched. The name on its side is Lighter, and Mr Okafor smiles as he hands Leila an oar.
Leila walks home, and she remembers five small steps that have helped her all summer. Notice the voice, pause for one breath, listen properly, give others the credit, and always begin again.
C1C2: Leila Haddad had won the argument, and everyone in the meeting room had seen her do it, with her figures neat and her voice calm and sure. Yet on the long walk home through the evening streets she felt strangely hollow, as though she had been handed a prize and then told it was made of paper. She could not have said why, and that puzzled her more than any defeat could have done.

At night she lay awake in the dark, playing the meeting again from the start like a film she had already seen a dozen times. She polished her best lines, added sharper replies to the things Dan had said, and cut out the moment when her voice had wobbled. It did not occur to her to ask who exactly she was performing for, since the only audience was the ceiling.

The next morning Dan stood at the front of the room and thanked Priya, warmly and publicly, for a clever idea that Leila was quite certain had been hers all along. Heat rose in her face, and a small, bitter voice in her head began to list everything she had done for the team that year. She smiled politely, but inside she was already keeping a careful and rather sulky account of who owed her what.

On Saturday morning she walked down to the harbour, hoping that the smell of salt and rope might clear her head. In the corner of the old Boatyard on Harbour Lane she found Mr Okafor, a retired boat builder with white hair and enormous patient hands, sanding the side of a small wooden boat. He glanced up, said good morning as though they had known each other for years, and went on working.

To her own surprise, Leila told the stranger the whole story, from the meeting to the sleepless night and the thanks that had gone to Priya. Mr Okafor listened without nodding or frowning, and when she finally ran out of words he let the silence sit for a moment. Then he asked, quite gently, who exactly it was that had felt so wounded.

Over two mugs of tea, Mr Okafor explained that everyone carries a kind of picture of who they are, made of labels, roles and opinions. Some people call this picture the Ego, although psychologists use the word in several other senses, and here it simply means the image of oneself that one feels must be protected. The picture is useful, he said, but it is only a picture, and a map is not the same thing as the land.

A small child learns first a name, then a place in the family, and then, very quickly, which behaviour earns a smile and which earns a frown. Little by little, through praise and blame and endless comparison with brothers, sisters and classmates, a picture of the self begins to grow, rather as a pearl forms around a speck of sand. Nobody plans this slow and quiet work, and most of us never notice it happening at all.

Mr Okafor handed her a pencil and asked her to write down every word she used to describe herself, and she was astonished at how quickly the page filled. Clever, reliable, organised, fair, the one who gets things done, and, underlined twice, the one who is right. It was a flattering portrait, and for the first time she wondered whether she had painted it herself.

A picture that feels fragile must be guarded constantly, Mr Okafor said, rather like a cracked jug carried carefully across a crowded yard. Every careless remark becomes an attack that must be answered, and every success becomes a small repair that keeps the whole thing from falling apart. Leila recognised the tiring vigilance at once, for she had lived inside it for years.

The self-image, Mr Okafor said, is always measuring, and it can only arrive at one of two answers: that I am better than you, or that I am worse. The odd thing is that both answers keep the attention firmly fixed on me, whether the mood is pride or shame. Leila laughed out loud, because she could think of days when she had managed to feel both before lunch.

Comparison, Mr Okafor said, is a ladder with no top, because however high you climb there is always somebody a rung or two above you. Even the people who seem to have everything look up at someone else, and so the climb never produces the rest it promises. Leila thought of Dan, and Priya, and a school friend who had since become famous, and felt tired just counting them.

Opinions can feel like parts of the body, Mr Okafor observed, which is why a simple disagreement can feel like a blow. We defend an idea as fiercely as we would defend a hand, even when it is a trivial idea, such as the best way to plane a plank, and even when we are not very sure of it. Leila remembered how hard she had fought in the meeting over a point she did not care about.

Her first task, Mr Okafor said, was not to change anything at all about herself or her habits. For one week she was simply to notice the voice in her head, as one might notice a radio playing in the next room, without arguing with it or trying to switch it off. She slipped a small notebook into her coat pocket, feeling oddly relieved that nothing more difficult was being asked of her that week.

On Monday morning, sitting on the crowded bus with her notebook open, Leila noticed something that she had never seen so clearly before. Without any decision on her part, her mind was passing judgement on everyone nearby, on the man's tired shoes, the girl's loud music, and the woman who took up too much of the seat. She wrote three words in her notebook, and the last of them, underlined, was embarrassment.

At her desk she caught herself composing the usual story about Dan, in which he was selfish, ambitious and secretly working against her. She stopped and looked at it, and saw that it was only a story, assembled out of two or three small events and a great deal of imagination. A thought can feel completely true and still be wrong, she wrote, and the sentence looked strange in her own handwriting.

Mr Okafor suggested that she give the voice a name, because something with a name is easier to see from a distance. After some thought Leila christened it the Lawyer, since it argued her case tirelessly from morning to night, and since it showed no interest whatever in what was actually true. It was a genuine relief, she found, to observe that the Lawyer was talking again, instead of simply believing every confident word.

The Lawyer, Leila discovered, had a thoroughly one-sided and rather tiresome way of working, like a tireless advocate who is paid only to win. It gathered every scrap of evidence in her favour, ignored anything that pointed the other way, and never once wondered whether Dan or Priya might have a case of their own. Seeing this did not silence the Lawyer, but it did make her a little less willing to accept its verdicts without question or hesitation.

The practice Mr Okafor offered was almost laughably small, which was exactly why she trusted it: before replying to anyone, take one slow breath. In that brief gap, he said, there is just enough room to choose a response, instead of letting the oldest habit in the house answer for you. At first she forgot it nine times in ten, but the tenth time felt like opening a window.

Her younger brother Sami rang on Wednesday evening, and within a minute he was complaining about his job. Leila's usual reply was a neat little lecture on what he ought to do, but this time she took a breath and said nothing at all. After a long pause he told her something he had never mentioned before, and she realised how many such things she had talked over without noticing.

Most of us, Mr Okafor remarked, do not listen so much as wait for a gap in which to talk. Real listening needs open space inside the listener, and there is very little room when the mind is busy preparing something clever to say. Leila decided to try an experiment, in which her only aim in each conversation was to hear one thing she had not known before.

A client sent Leila a glowing email on Thursday, and she carried the warm feeling around for most of the afternoon. By evening it had faded, and she noticed, with some alarm, that she was already hoping for the next compliment. Praise is pleasant weather, Mr Okafor said, but a person who depends on the weather will never feel safe in a house with no roof.

A senior manager criticised her latest report in front of two colleagues, and it stung far more than the facts deserved. Leila could feel the Lawyer clearing its throat, but she asked herself instead whether any part of the criticism was true. To her annoyance, about a third of it was, and the report improved once she admitted that.

Mr Okafor told her about his first boatyard, which he had built with great pride in his twenties and lost within five years. He had never understood the accounts, and he had been far too proud to say so, and so the debts had grown quietly while he went on building beautiful boats. It was the best lesson of his life, he said, though he would not wish its price on anyone.

On Friday morning Leila did something she had avoided for years, and asked Priya, a junior colleague, to show her how a difficult spreadsheet worked. Her heart thumped, and the Lawyer muttered that she was giving away her authority, but the words came out all the same. Priya looked startled, then pleased, and within ten minutes the whole problem was solved.

Priya was delighted to be asked, and the two women ended up laughing over the strange habits of the spreadsheet. It struck Leila that asking for help had not made her smaller in anyone's eyes, and that it had handed Priya a small gift, the chance to feel useful. The Lawyer, she noted, had assumed the exact opposite and had been wrong, as usual.

An old friend from university announced a remarkable promotion, and Leila, to her dismay, felt a sharp twist of envy beneath her congratulations. She had always thought of herself as a generous person, and for a moment the Lawyer tried to explain the feeling away. Instead she decided to look at it squarely, the way Mr Okafor would inspect a suspicious patch of damp in a plank.

When she watched the envy calmly, without feeling guilty about it, it gradually revealed its meaning, as a pointing finger reveals a direction. It showed her what she wanted, which was more freedom and less hurry in her working life, and that was something she could act upon. Envy, she wrote, is not a verdict on my character but a piece of information about my wishes.

Humility, Mr Okafor said, is often misunderstood as a kind of low opinion of oneself, when it is nearer to a low level of self-preoccupation. A humble person is not busy thinking badly of herself, but thinking about herself rather less, which leaves a great deal more attention free for the people and the work in front of her. Leila thought that this sounded like a considerable relief rather than a painful sacrifice, and she wondered why nobody had put it to her like that before.

Leila had always believed that her harsh inner criticism kept her sharp, and she was reluctant to give it up. Mr Okafor pointed out that self-hatred is simply the ego in a gloomier costume, since the whole attention is still fixed on me and my failings. A stern voice may feel like honesty, he said, but honest advice is usually kind enough to be believed.

On a hurried Tuesday, Leila sent an important report to a client and discovered an hour later that one of the key figures was wrong. Her stomach dropped, and almost at once the Lawyer began to prepare a list of the people and circumstances that might share the blame. It was an old and well-rehearsed routine, and she knew every step of it by heart.

This time Leila took a long breath, allowed the Lawyer to finish its speech without believing a word of it, and wrote to the client in plain language. She admitted the error, supplied the correct figure and apologised once, briefly, without any elaborate explanation. It was one of the shortest and most uncomfortable emails she had ever written, and it took her only four minutes.

To her amazement, the client was not angry in the slightest, and he thanked her for the speed and honesty of her message. He told her, rather kindly, that he trusted people who admitted errors far more than people who claimed never to make any, and Leila felt something loosen in her chest. She had spent years protecting a picture that nobody else had ever demanded she keep.

In the next team meeting, Leila put Priya's name on the front of the slide and described her analysis, aloud and in detail, as the best piece of work that month. She had expected a pang of loss, and instead she felt lighter, as though a heavy bag she had carried for years had slid from her shoulder. Priya blushed and grinned from ear to ear, and the whole room seemed to grow a good deal warmer.

No boat builder in history has ever controlled the sea, Mr Okafor said, and the best of them have never tried. The ancient Stoic teachers, such as Epictetus, made a similar point when they separated the things that are up to us, like our choices and attitudes, from the many things that are not. Leila wrote the distinction at the top of a clean page and noticed how often she wasted her strength on the second list.

Leila's mother arrived on Saturday with a suitcase, a casserole and a very slight lift of one eyebrow. Within an hour Leila was behaving like a defensive teenager, snapping at remarks about her cooking and her curtains that were probably not meant as attacks at all. It was astonishing, she wrote that night, how fast an old role can climb back into its favourite chair.

Roles are useful, said Mr Okafor, because the world needs managers, daughters, neighbours and friends, and it would be foolish to refuse to play them. The trouble begins only when we forget that a role is something we do and not everything we are, and then a change of role feels like a kind of death. Leila thought of the three or four hats she wore each day, and wondered who it was that kept putting them on.

In August a rumour began to travel around the office, and then an email confirmed it: the company was planning a reorganisation, and nobody could say who would keep which job. Leila felt every old fear awaken at once, and the loudest of them was not about money but about her title. Without it, she thought, she would hardly know how to introduce herself at a party.

That evening she asked herself a question she had always avoided, which was what would remain if the title, the labels and the reputation were all taken away. After a long, slow walk along the sea wall she wrote three answers in her notebook: what she valued, whom she cared about, and what she gave her attention to. They were not impressive answers, but they were hers, and no reorganisation could touch them.

Beneath the fear of losing her job lay a deeper and older one, which was the fear of being nobody at all. Yet as she stood there with the cold wind in her face, Leila noticed that she was breathing, thinking, noticing and caring, and that this was already a great deal to be going on with. Nobody, she decided with a small, surprised laugh, was a rather odd description for someone so thoroughly and obviously alive.

At dawn on a Sunday, Mr Okafor invited Leila to take the oars and row him out beyond the harbour wall. For a long time neither of them spoke, and the only sounds were the creak of the rowlocks, the drip of the blades and the occasional cry of a gull. It was the first time in months that she had spent an hour without trying to be anyone in particular.

Out on the water the sky seemed enormous, pink and gold at its edges, and Leila felt very small beneath it. Strangely, the feeling was not frightening but restful, as though a muscle she had been clenching for years had finally been allowed to relax. Some studies suggest that awe turns attention outward and makes people a little more generous, though the results vary, and Leila did not need an experiment to tell her what she felt.

When Leila asked a hard question about the tides, Mr Okafor said cheerfully that he did not know, and that he had been wondering about it for forty years. Far from losing her respect, the answer raised it, because it was the sort of honest ignorance that keeps a mind open and curious. She resolved to say the same three words at work, at least once a week, and to see what happened.

One evening, when Mr Okafor had gone home early with a cold, Leila stayed behind in the boatyard and sanded a long plank on the little boat's hull. Nobody was watching, nobody would ever thank her, and she resolved not to mention it, which was a real test of her resolve. The work was slow and simple, and she was astonished by how deeply she enjoyed it.

In a tense meeting about the new plan, Leila did something that would have been unthinkable in June, and said aloud, in front of everyone, that she had been wrong. She had feared that respect would drain out of the room, but instead the shoulders around the table dropped and the conversation became more honest than any she had heard that year. Dan even smiled at her across the table, and she smiled back warmly, without stopping to calculate what it might mean.

A few days later, tired and late and carrying too many bags, Leila snapped rudely at a stranger who had stopped in front of her in the supermarket queue. She felt the familiar heat of self-righteousness, followed by the cold wash of shame, and she walked home wondering whether the whole summer's work had been for nothing. The Lawyer, naturally, had a great deal to say on the subject, and most of it was extremely unkind.

Leila confessed the whole story of the queue, and Mr Okafor laughed, kindly and without the slightest surprise. Falling back is not a failure of the practice, he said, because it is the practice, and the only useful response is to forgive yourself, notice what happened and begin again. He had been beginning again for seventy years, he added, and expected to go on doing so until the end.

Nobody can throw the ego away, Mr Okafor told her, and it would not be wise to try, because the same machinery also helps us to plan, to protect ourselves and to get through a working day. The aim is to hold it like a rope in the hand, firmly enough to be useful and loosely enough to let go when it pulls. Many traditions, from Buddhist and Christian to Sufi and Stoic, have taught this idea in their own words and in their own ways.

In early September the reorganisation was finally announced, and Leila was offered a new role leading a smaller and more varied team. The old Leila would have counted the rungs of her title and complained about every one that she had lost, but this Leila asked only whether the work was good and whether she could learn from it. She said yes at once, without bargaining, and was quietly surprised to find that she was smiling.

At the end of the summer, the little wooden boat was finished, and half the harbour came down to watch it slide into the water. On its bow, in plain white paint, was the name Lighter, which Mr Okafor said was both a joke and a hope. He handed Leila an oar without a word, and she took it as one takes a small, important responsibility.

Leila walked home along the harbour in the last of the light, and she counted five small steps on her fingers, as she had learned to do all summer. Notice the voice, pause for one breath, listen properly, give others their credit, and begin again whenever you fall. None of it was dramatic, she thought, but the evening felt lighter, and for once nobody inside her head was arguing with it.
